purpose: Plan, structure, draft, clarify, format, visualize, review, and release clear written and professional communication so a defined reader can make a decision or take an action; modeled as concrete, evaluable writing/communication work-units for a knowledge-searcher meta-KB.
assumptions: subdomain of Professional Communication & Speaking; scope is written and document-based workplace communication
no observed dataset supplied; all numeric values are heuristic priors
nodes are concrete writing/communication work-units, not abstract principles
decision-oriented business and technical communication is the primary frame
exclusions: live oral delivery, public speaking, and voice/body performance
real-time conversation, negotiation, and meeting facilitation
graphic design and brand identity beyond document and slide clarity
natural-language generation modeling and linguistics theory for its own sake

competency_questions.question: Who is the reader, what decision must this communication produce, and what single message carries it?
What is the one governing claim and how is the supporting content grouped beneath it?
How is the document structured top-down so the answer comes first and the logic is traceable?
Can a decision-maker act from the summary or report alone, and does the body support it?
Is the prose clear and concise enough to be understood and read completely on first pass?
Are language, tone, terminology, and detail calibrated to this specific reader and channel?
Does the message put the ask up front with a clear next step for the recipient?
Is every major claim backed by attributable, verifiable evidence?
Does the proposal present a recommended option against alternatives with a justified cost/benefit case?
Is reference content findable, task-complete, and maintainable over time?
Do slides and charts make the intended point obvious without distorting the data?
Does each visual encode the intended comparison with graphical integrity?
Has the communication been reviewed, reconciled with feedback, and approved before release?

glossary.definition: 'bottom line up front': stating the conclusion or ask before its support
a top-down structure where a governing answer is supported by grouped, summarizing arguments
mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive grouping of ideas
a standalone synopsis delivering the recommendation and ask for decision without the body
the leading sentence of a paragraph that states its single point
direct, jargon-free wording recoverable on first read
the level of formality and tone fitted to context and relationship
an explicit statement of what the reader should do next
faithful data encoding where visual magnitude matches data magnitude
a slide title that states the slide's point as a full claim
the recorded approval required before a communication is released

evidence_label_policy.note: No observed/experimental inputs supplied; only heuristic labels are eligible.

source_registry.description: Heuristic priors from established business- and technical-writing literature (Minto 'The Minto Pyramid Principle' 1996; Heath & Heath 'Made to Stick' 2007; Williams & Bizup 'Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace'; Tufte on data display; plain-language guidance) and professional editorial practice; no measured dataset supplied.
grounding_limits: all numeric values are heuristic priors, not measurements
no observed or experimentally_validated labels are eligible

normalization_definitions.rounding: round computed scores to 2 decimals; tolerance 0.02

nodes.definition: Determine who the reader is, what decision or action the document must produce, and the single message it must carry before any drafting begins.
contradictors: writer who drafts before knowing the reader

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the reader, the decision being asked for, or the channel changes

pros.claim: every downstream choice (structure, tone, length) is anchored to a real reader and a real decision
pros.example: writing an exec a one-page recommendation rather than a full technical log

cons.claim: front-loaded analysis feels slow for trivial messages
cons.example: spending audience analysis on a one-line scheduling reply

acceptance_tests: audience profile names the decision-maker and the action sought
one governing message is stated in a single sentence
revisit_triggers: channel changes (email vs slide vs report)
purpose reframed from inform to persuade

nodes.definition: Compress the communication into one governing claim (the answer) that the whole document exists to deliver and defend.
contradictors: writer who buries the point in the middle

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the recommendation or the core ask changes

pros.claim: a single defensible message prevents diffuse, unmemorable documents
pros.example: Made-to-Stick concreteness makes the ask repeatable by the reader

cons.claim: forcing one message can oversimplify genuinely multi-decision documents
cons.example: collapsing three independent budget asks into one blurred line

failure_modes: message too abstract to act on
acceptance_tests: exactly one governing message is recorded
message survives a 'so what / why care' test

nodes.definition: Arrange content top-down so the answer comes first, supported by grouped, mutually-exclusive arguments that each summarize the ideas beneath them.
contradictors: writer who builds bottom-up to a buried conclusion

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a supporting group is added, removed, or proven non-MECE

pros.claim: answer-first structure lets busy readers stop early with the decision in hand
pros.example: Minto pyramid: recommendation in line one, support grouped beneath

cons.claim: rigid pyramids can feel blunt for narrative or relationship-building writing
cons.example: a condolence or vision piece forced into bullet logic

acceptance_tests: the answer appears before its support
supporting groups are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive
revisit_triggers: reader reports they could not find the point

nodes.definition: Open with Situation, Complication, Question, Answer so the reader shares the problem context before receiving the recommendation.
contradictors: writer who opens with background dump

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the framing context or the triggering complication changes

pros.claim: shared problem framing makes the answer feel earned rather than asserted
pros.example: SCQA lead lets a sponsor see why the decision is needed now

cons.claim: over-long situation sections delay the answer
cons.example: three paragraphs of background before any point

acceptance_tests: introduction contains a complication and a question
the answer matches the document key message

nodes.definition: Produce a standalone summary that delivers the recommendation, rationale, and ask so a decision can be made without reading the body.
contradictors: writer who treats the summary as an intro teaser

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the recommendation, its support, or the ask changes

pros.claim: decision-makers can act from the summary alone, the most-read part of any document
pros.example: a board approves from the one-pager without opening the deck

cons.claim: summaries written before the body drift out of sync with it
cons.example: a summary promising a conclusion the body never reaches

acceptance_tests: the summary states the recommendation and the ask
a reader of only the summary can make the decision

nodes.definition: Lead each paragraph with its point and connect paragraphs so the argument advances in a traceable line.
contradictors: writer who hides the point at paragraph end

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when paragraphs are reordered or merged

pros.claim: reading the first sentence of each paragraph reconstructs the whole argument
pros.example: a skim of topic sentences yields the document's logic

cons.claim: mechanical topic sentences can flatten nuanced prose
cons.example: every paragraph starting with a formulaic claim

acceptance_tests: first sentences alone convey the argument
each paragraph links to the previous via old-to-new
revisit_triggers: a section is split or merged

nodes.definition: Replace jargon, nominalizations, and convoluted syntax with direct verbs and concrete subjects so meaning is recoverable on first read.
contradictors: writer who equates complexity with credibility

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the audience reading level or domain-jargon tolerance changes

pros.claim: first-read comprehension rises and reader effort falls
pros.example: 'we will decide by Friday' instead of 'a determination will be effectuated')

cons.claim: over-simplification can strip needed technical precision
cons.example: flattening a legal term of art into a vague paraphrase

acceptance_tests: no unexplained jargon for the target reader
sentences average active, verb-led constructions
revisit_triggers: domain term must be preserved exactly

nodes.definition: Cut redundancy, hedging, and filler so every sentence earns its place without losing necessary content.
contradictors: writer who pads to appear thorough

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a length limit changes or content is added

pros.claim: shorter documents are read more completely and faster
pros.example: cutting a 2-page memo to 3 paragraphs lifts its read rate

cons.claim: aggressive cutting can delete necessary caveats or nuance
cons.example: removing a risk caveat to hit a word count

acceptance_tests: no sentence can be removed without losing meaning
length meets the stated constraint

nodes.definition: Adjust depth, terminology, examples, and framing to the specific reader's expertise, role, and stake.
contradictors: writer who uses one version for all readers

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the document is repurposed for a different reader

pros.claim: the same facts land correctly for engineers and executives alike
pros.example: a technical fix summarized as risk-and-cost for finance

cons.claim: per-audience versions multiply maintenance and drift risk
cons.example: three diverging copies of one policy

acceptance_tests: terminology matches the reader's expertise
omitted detail is justified by reader need
revisit_triggers: document reused for a new audience

nodes.definition: Set a tone (formality, warmth, directness) appropriate to the relationship, stakes, and channel without misrepresenting content.
contradictors: writer who uses identical tone in every context

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the relationship, stakes, or channel changes

pros.claim: appropriate tone preserves relationships while still being direct
pros.example: a firm-but-warm escalation that does not burn the relationship

cons.claim: tone errors are hard to detect by the author and can offend silently
cons.example: unintended curtness reading as hostility over email

failure_modes: tone too cold or too casual for stakes
acceptance_tests: tone matches relationship and channel
an unwelcome message is still unambiguous

nodes.definition: Write action-oriented email with a precise subject, the ask up front, scannable body, and a clear next step.
contradictors: writer who buries the ask in paragraph four

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when recipients, the ask, or the deadline changes

pros.claim: the reader knows what to do within the first two lines
pros.example: subject 'Approval needed by Thu: vendor X' with the ask first

cons.claim: over-templated email can feel curt or transactional
cons.example: a terse ask with no context to an external partner

acceptance_tests: the ask and deadline appear in the first lines
subject line predicts the action needed

nodes.definition: Build a structured report with executive summary, scoped findings, and evidence so a reader can both decide and verify.
contradictors: writer who dumps raw analysis without a summary

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when findings, evidence, or the recommendation change

pros.claim: readers can stop at the summary or drill into verifiable detail
pros.example: a recommendation report whose appendix lets a skeptic check the numbers

cons.claim: full reports are costly and over-used where a memo would do
cons.example: a 20-page report for a decision a one-pager could carry

acceptance_tests: summary is decision-ready and standalone
each finding traces to evidence

nodes.definition: Construct a proposal that frames a problem, presents a recommended option against alternatives, and justifies the ask with benefits and costs.
contradictors: writer who lists features without a decision case

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the recommended option, its cost, or the decision criteria change

pros.claim: a clear recommendation against alternatives makes approval low-effort
pros.example: a one-option-recommended proposal with costs and objections pre-answered

cons.claim: persuasive framing can slide into overclaiming or hiding risk
cons.example: downplaying a known cost to win approval

acceptance_tests: the recommended option and its cost are explicit
major objections are addressed in-text

nodes.definition: Write durable reference content (how-tos, specs, policies) optimized for retrieval, task completion, and maintenance over time.
contradictors: writer who treats docs as write-once

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the documented system or its tasks change

pros.claim: users self-serve and find answers without asking the author
pros.example: a how-to that lets a new hire complete the task unaided

cons.claim: stale documentation is worse than none and decays silently
cons.example: a setup guide referencing a removed menu option

acceptance_tests: a target user can complete the task from the doc alone
each doc has an owner and a review date
revisit_triggers: support tickets reveal a doc gap

nodes.definition: Communicate progress, risks, and asks on a recurring cadence so stakeholders stay aligned without meetings.
contradictors: writer who reports activity instead of outcomes

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when scope, schedule, or risk status changes materially

pros.claim: stakeholders self-serve status and only engage on real risks
pros.example: a red/amber/green update that surfaces one blocker needing a decision

cons.claim: reporting activity rather than outcomes creates noise
cons.example: a list of tasks done with no statement of whether the goal is on track

acceptance_tests: update states on/off-track against a target
each blocker carries an owner and an ask

nodes.definition: Apply a consistent style (terminology, formatting, mechanics) across a document or set so the reader is not distracted by variation.
contradictors: writer who varies terms for the same concept

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the style guide or product terminology changes

pros.claim: consistent terms and formatting reduce reader friction and ambiguity
pros.example: one product name spelled the same way throughout a doc set

cons.claim: rigid style enforcement can slow drafting and feel pedantic
cons.example: blocking a draft over a serial-comma preference

acceptance_tests: each concept has one consistent term
formatting follows the style guide

nodes.definition: Design slides with one idea per slide, assertion-style headlines, and minimal supporting visuals to aid a spoken or read narrative.
contradictors: writer who pastes paragraphs onto slides

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the storyline or the underlying recommendation changes

pros.claim: assertion headlines let a deck be read and understood without the speaker
pros.example: reading only the slide titles reconstructs the argument

cons.claim: slideware tempts oversimplification and bullet-point thinking
cons.example: a complex tradeoff reduced to three bullets that mislead

failure_modes: decorative visuals that add no information
acceptance_tests: each slide carries one idea stated in its headline
titles alone convey the storyline

nodes.definition: Choose and design chart types and tables that make the intended comparison obvious and avoid distorting the data.
contradictors: writer who picks charts for decoration

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when the data or the intended comparison changes

pros.claim: the right chart makes the key comparison readable in seconds
pros.example: a slope chart that shows the trend a table would hide

cons.claim: misleading scales or chart choices can distort or deceive
cons.example: a truncated y-axis exaggerating a small difference

acceptance_tests: the chart makes the intended comparison obvious
encodings (axes, scale) are not misleading

nodes.definition: Select, attribute, and weave supporting evidence into claims so each assertion is backed and verifiable without overwhelming the reader.
contradictors: writer who asserts without support

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a claim's supporting evidence is added, removed, or contradicted

pros.claim: every claim a skeptical reader could challenge is pre-supported
pros.example: a recommendation each line of which cites a verifiable source

cons.claim: over-citing buries the argument in supporting detail
cons.example: footnotes that outweigh the point being made

acceptance_tests: each major claim links to attributable evidence
contradicting evidence is acknowledged

nodes.definition: Run a final accuracy, consistency, and correctness pass and obtain required approvals before a communication is released.
contradictors: writer who sends without a final pass

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when content changes after a prior review or a new error class is found

pros.claim: errors are caught before they reach the reader, where they are costly to retract
pros.example: a wrong figure caught before a board sees it

cons.claim: review can become a bottleneck or rubber-stamp under time pressure
cons.example: skipping the number-check to hit a send deadline

acceptance_tests: all numbers and names are verified against source
required approvals are recorded before release
revisit_triggers: a new error type is discovered

nodes.definition: Collect, reconcile, and apply reviewer feedback while preserving the document's message and resolving conflicting comments.
contradictors: writer who applies every comment literally

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: when a new review round or conflicting feedback arrives

pros.claim: feedback improves the document without diluting its core message
pros.example: reconciling two reviewers' opposite edits by returning to the purpose

cons.claim: applying all comments literally can fragment the message
cons.example: a document rewritten into committee mush

acceptance_tests: each comment is accepted, rejected, or merged with a reason
the key message survives revision

edges.why_related: the key message is derived from who the reader is and what decision is sought
edges.benefit_of_coupling: message anchored to a real reader
edges.risk_of_conflict: message set before audience known drifts
edges.example: define audience, then the one message

edges.why_related: the pyramid is built to support and lead with the key message
edges.risk_of_conflict: structuring before a message yields a buried lede
edges.example: fix the message, then group support

edges.why_related: the SCQA answer IS the key message
edges.benefit_of_coupling: opening lands on the agreed message
edges.risk_of_conflict: SCQA without a message has no answer
edges.example: set the answer, then frame the lead

edges.why_related: the summary distills the top of the argument tree
edges.risk_of_conflict: summarizing an unstable tree forces rewrites
edges.example: build the tree, then summarize it

edges.why_related: paragraph topic sentences realize the argument groups
edges.risk_of_conflict: writing paragraphs before grouping causes reordering

edges.why_related: slide headlines instantiate the argument tree as a storyline
edges.risk_of_conflict: designing slides before structure yields incoherent decks

edges.why_related: evidence is attached to the structured claims
edges.risk_of_conflict: integrating evidence before structure scatters it

edges.why_related: the report is assembled around the executive summary
edges.benefit_of_coupling: report leads with a decision-ready summary
edges.risk_of_conflict: writing the body first desynchronizes the summary

edges.why_related: paragraph-level structure should be set before sentence-level plain-language edits
edges.benefit_of_coupling: clarity edits work on stable paragraphs
edges.risk_of_conflict: plain-language editing before flow wastes effort on reordered text

edges.why_related: clarify wording before cutting length so cuts do not remove needed meaning
edges.risk_of_conflict: cutting before clarifying can delete real content

edges.why_related: adaptation tunes already-plain text to the specific reader
edges.benefit_of_coupling: adaptation builds on a clear baseline
edges.risk_of_conflict: adapting unclear text compounds confusion
edges.example: make it clear, then tune to reader

edges.why_related: adaptation requires the audience profile produced by framing
edges.benefit_of_coupling: adaptation uses a real reader model
edges.risk_of_conflict: adapting without a reader model is guesswork

edges.why_related: tone is calibrated to the adapted reader and relationship
edges.risk_of_conflict: setting tone before knowing the reader misfires

edges.why_related: email leads with the key ask derived from the message
edges.risk_of_conflict: email without a message has no clear ask
edges.example: set the ask, then write the email

edges.why_related: email tone is set by the calibrated register
edges.risk_of_conflict: ungauged tone in email offends silently

edges.why_related: report sections rely on paragraph-level flow
edges.benefit_of_coupling: report reads as a connected argument
edges.risk_of_conflict: disconnected paragraphs make reports incoherent

edges.why_related: the proposal's recommendation is the key message
edges.risk_of_conflict: a proposal without a message has no recommendation

edges.why_related: the proposal's benefit/cost case must rest on integrated evidence
edges.benefit_of_coupling: claims in the ask are backed
edges.risk_of_conflict: an unbacked proposal overclaims
edges.example: integrate evidence, then make the ask

edges.why_related: report findings must be supported by integrated evidence
edges.risk_of_conflict: unsupported findings undermine the report

edges.why_related: documentation must be plain to be usable as reference
edges.benefit_of_coupling: docs are usable on first read
edges.risk_of_conflict: jargon-heavy docs fail self-service

edges.why_related: reference doc sets require consistent terminology to be findable
edges.risk_of_conflict: inconsistent terms fragment docs

edges.why_related: a status update leads with the on/off-track message
edges.risk_of_conflict: activity-dump updates lack a message

edges.why_related: chart choice depends on the intended comparison and reader
edges.risk_of_conflict: reader-blind charts mislead

edges.why_related: slides embed the designed data displays
edges.risk_of_conflict: slides with raw/wrong charts mislead live
edges.example: design charts, then place on slides

edges.why_related: final proofreading follows the last content edit
edges.risk_of_conflict: proofing before edits finish wastes the pass

edges.why_related: the review pass verifies consistency was applied
edges.risk_of_conflict: skipping consistency leaves visible variation
edges.example: apply style, then verify in review

edges.why_related: review verifies that claims and numbers match their evidence
edges.risk_of_conflict: unchecked numbers reach readers

edges.why_related: feedback is gathered on a drafted report
edges.benefit_of_coupling: revision works on a real draft
edges.risk_of_conflict: reviewing nothing yields no feedback

edges.why_related: the final proof follows feedback reconciliation
edges.benefit_of_coupling: proof runs on the reconciled draft
edges.risk_of_conflict: proofing before feedback is applied is wasted

edges.why_related: a single sharp message competes with full evidentiary completeness
edges.risk_of_conflict: either an oversimplified ask or an evidence-buried point
edges.example: one-line ask vs every caveat included
edges.resolution_rule: lead with the message; relegate full evidence to support/appendix

edges.why_related: cutting length conflicts with including all supporting evidence
edges.risk_of_conflict: cuts can drop needed support or length can bloat with citations
edges.example: trimming a memo vs keeping every source
edges.resolution_rule: keep evidence that backs decision-critical claims; move the rest to appendix

edges.why_related: brevity competes with adding reader-specific explanation
edges.risk_of_conflict: too short for novices or too padded for experts
edges.example: cutting context a new reader needs
edges.resolution_rule: tailor length to the reader; brevity yields when comprehension is at risk

edges.why_related: maximal plainness can clash with required formality or warmth
edges.risk_of_conflict: blunt plainness reads as cold, or formality obscures meaning
edges.example: a curt plain sentence to a sensitive stakeholder
edges.resolution_rule: preserve clarity; adjust tone within the bounds of unambiguous meaning

edges.why_related: persuasive framing competes with balanced evidentiary honesty
edges.risk_of_conflict: overclaiming benefits or hiding risks
edges.example: downplaying a known cost to win approval
edges.resolution_rule: evidence integrity dominates; persuasion may frame but not misrepresent

edges.why_related: slide simplicity competes with faithful data representation
edges.risk_of_conflict: over-simplified visuals distort the data
edges.resolution_rule: graphical integrity dominates; simplify presentation, not the data

edges.why_related: the standalone summary can diverge from the evolving body
edges.benefit_of_coupling: balances summary stability against body changes
edges.risk_of_conflict: summary and body assert different conclusions
edges.example: summary promises what the body never concludes
edges.resolution_rule: reconcile to the body; the summary must not outrun the evidence

edges.why_related: a failed final review can reveal the message itself was wrong and trigger a re-frame
edges.risk_of_conflict: endless re-messaging loops
edges.example: review finds the recommendation is indefensible
edges.resolution_rule: revisit the message only on material defect; stop after one re-frame per review round

edges.why_related: reviewer feedback can require restructuring the argument tree
edges.risk_of_conflict: perpetual restructuring on minor comments
edges.example: a reviewer shows two groups overlap
edges.resolution_rule: restructure only for non-MECE or logic defects; stop when groups are MECE

edges.why_related: charting can expose that the underlying evidence does not support the claim
edges.risk_of_conflict: re-charting loops without resolution
edges.example: a chart shows the trend is not significant
edges.resolution_rule: revise the claim or evidence once exposed; stop when chart and claim agree

edges.why_related: both produce structured long-form documents but serve decision vs reference purposes
edges.benefit_of_coupling: shared structuring and clarity skills transfer
edges.risk_of_conflict: conflating a one-time report with durable reference docs
edges.example: reusing report style for a maintained wiki page
edges.resolution_rule: treat as distinct artifact classes; share skills, not lifecycle

conflict_axes.trigger: delivering one sharp message conflicts with including every supporting detail
resolution_order: lead with the message and decision-critical evidence
move exhaustive support to appendices
cut only non-decision-critical detail
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: clarity governs the main line; completeness is preserved in support layers, never deleted
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if cutting would remove a decision-critical caveat
conflict_axes.example: the message becomes unactionable without the omitted detail

conflict_axes.trigger: framing to win approval conflicts with presenting costs and risks honestly
resolution_order: state benefits and the recommended option
disclose costs, risks, and alternatives
let framing organize but not distort the facts
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: evidentiary honesty dominates; persuasion may frame but never misrepresent or omit material risk
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if a known material risk or cost would be hidden to win approval
conflict_axes.example: a stakeholder relies on a claim the evidence does not support

conflict_axes.trigger: reducing visual noise conflicts with faithfully representing the data
resolution_order: choose the chart that shows the intended comparison
keep axes and scales honest
simplify presentation, not the underlying data
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: graphical integrity dominates; simplify chrome and labels, never the data encoding
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if simplification truncates scales or hides variance
conflict_axes.example: a viewer would draw a conclusion the full data contradicts

conflict_axes.trigger: maximal directness can damage a relationship that requires warmth or diplomacy
resolution_order: keep the core message unambiguous
adjust tone for the relationship and stakes
never soften to the point of ambiguity
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: clarity of message dominates; tone is tuned within the bounds of an unambiguous message
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if softening would make the message ambiguous or evasive
conflict_axes.example: the reader cannot tell what is being asked or said

conflict_axes.trigger: pressure to send fast conflicts with verifying accuracy and obtaining sign-off
resolution_order: scale review to stakes and irreversibility
always verify numbers, names, and external claims
obtain required approvals before external release
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: review dominates for high-stakes or external communication; speed is allowed only for low-risk internal notes
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if an unverified number or claim would reach an external or executive reader
conflict_axes.example: the communication is irreversible or high-visibility

conflict_axes.trigger: a standalone summary written early can diverge from an evolving body
resolution_order: draft the summary from the validated structure
re-reconcile the summary after body changes
never let the summary claim more than the body proves
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: the body of evidence dominates; the summary is re-synced to it before release
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if the summary asserts a conclusion the body does not reach
conflict_axes.example: reader of the summary alone would be misled

conflict_axes.trigger: tailoring per audience conflicts with maintaining one consistent canonical source
resolution_order: keep one canonical source of truth
derive audience versions from it
track divergence and reconcile on change
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: consistency of the canonical source dominates; adaptations are derived views, not forks
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if audience versions diverge into conflicting facts
conflict_axes.example: a reader receives information that contradicts the canonical source

conflict_axes.trigger: strict answer-first structure can suppress narrative needed to engage or persuade
resolution_order: default to answer-first for decision documents
allow narrative framing in the opening
keep the governing message recoverable regardless
conflict_axes.dominance_logic: structure dominates for decision documents; narrative is permitted in framing where it aids engagement without burying the answer
conflict_axes.escalation_threshold: if narrative framing buries the recommendation
conflict_axes.example: a busy reader cannot find the point quickly

edge_cases.trigger: the answer is placed after long background
edge_cases.failure_mode: buried lede; reader misses the point
edge_cases.example: a memo whose ask is in the final paragraph
edge_cases.detection_method: check whether the recommendation/answer appears before its support
resolution: move the answer to the top

edge_cases.trigger: persuasive framing asserts beyond the evidence
edge_cases.example: claiming ROI with no cited basis
edge_cases.detection_method: trace each benefit claim to attributable evidence and flag unsupported ones
resolution: downgrade claim to what evidence supports
disclose the risk or cost omitted

edge_cases.trigger: axis truncation or wrong chart type exaggerates a difference
edge_cases.example: a truncated y-axis turning a 2% change into a visual doubling
edge_cases.detection_method: check axis baselines, scales, and chart-type fit to the comparison
resolution: choose a chart that matches the comparison

edge_cases.trigger: the document is written for the wrong reader or register
edge_cases.failure_mode: audience mismatch; message does not land
edge_cases.example: sending a deep technical log to a finance approver
edge_cases.detection_method: verify the audience profile names the actual decision-maker and the draft matches it

edge_cases.trigger: reference content describes a removed or changed system
edge_cases.failure_mode: stale source grounding; doc misleads users
edge_cases.example: a setup guide citing a deprecated menu
edge_cases.detection_method: compare doc against current system state and last review date
resolution: assign an owner to maintain it

edge_cases.trigger: a number or name is released without verification
edge_cases.example: a wrong revenue figure in a board pack
edge_cases.detection_method: reconcile every figure and proper noun against its source before release
resolution: add a verification step to the review gate

edge_cases.trigger: the summary asserts a conclusion the body never reaches
edge_cases.example: a one-pager promising savings the analysis does not show
edge_cases.detection_method: compare the summary's recommendation and ask against the body
resolution: re-sync the summary to the body

edge_cases.trigger: applying every comment literally fragments the message
edge_cases.example: a document rewritten into contradictory mush
edge_cases.detection_method: after revision, test that the governing message still holds

edge_cases.trigger: the message states information but no explicit next step
edge_cases.failure_mode: missing call to action; no reader response
edge_cases.example: an update with no decision requested
edge_cases.detection_method: check the message contains an explicit ask and owner/deadline
resolution: add an explicit ask with owner and deadline

edge_cases.trigger: aggressive cutting deletes a needed caveat or precise term
edge_cases.example: cutting a risk caveat to hit a word count
edge_cases.detection_method: diff the tightened text against the prior for dropped caveats or terms of art

edge_cases.trigger: supporting groups overlap or leave gaps
edge_cases.example: two sections both arguing the same point
edge_cases.detection_method: test each supporting group for mutual exclusivity and collective exhaustiveness

workflow.objective: fix the reader, the decision, and the single governing message
acceptance_tests: audience profile names decision-maker and action
exactly one governing message recorded
workflow.do_first_because: nothing downstream is valid unless the reader, decision, and message are fixed first

workflow.objective: build the top-down argument tree and attach supporting evidence
acceptance_tests: answer precedes support
groups are MECE
each major claim is backed
workflow.do_first_because: structuring before drafting prevents reordering and buried-lede rework

workflow.objective: produce a standalone, decision-ready executive summary
acceptance_tests: summary states recommendation and ask
summary readable without the body
workflow.do_first_because: the most-read artifact must be anchored to the validated structure, not drafted ad hoc

workflow.objective: draft body paragraphs led by their points and connected by transitions
acceptance_tests: first sentences alone convey the argument
paragraphs link old-to-new
exit_criteria: body draft reads as a connected argument
workflow.do_first_because: paragraph-level flow must be set before sentence-level edits to avoid reworking moved text

workflow.objective: make the prose plain and concise without losing meaning
acceptance_tests: no unexplained jargon for the reader
no removable sentence remains
exit_criteria: draft is clear, concise, and within length
workflow.do_first_because: clarify before cutting so concision does not delete needed content

workflow.objective: calibrate depth, tone, and terminology to the specific reader and channel
acceptance_tests: terminology matches reader expertise
tone fits relationship and channel
terms used consistently
exit_criteria: draft tuned to reader and channel
workflow.do_first_because: tuning after clarity avoids re-editing the same text twice

workflow.objective: render the content into the chosen document format with format-specific conventions
acceptance_tests: format conventions applied
an explicit ask/next step is present
exit_criteria: document is in the correct format with a clear ask
workflow.do_first_because: format is applied after content is stable so format work is not redone

workflow.objective: produce slides and charts that carry the storyline with graphical integrity
acceptance_tests: each slide carries one idea in its headline
encodings are not misleading
workflow.do_first_because: visuals follow stable content so charts are not rebuilt after edits

workflow.objective: collect and reconcile feedback while preserving the governing message
acceptance_tests: each comment accepted/rejected/merged with a reason
governing message survives revision
workflow.do_first_because: reconcile feedback before the final proof so proofing runs once on stable text

workflow.objective: verify accuracy and consistency, obtain sign-off, and release
acceptance_tests: all numbers and names verified against source
required approvals recorded
exit_criteria: document verified and approved for release
workflow.do_first_because: final verification and human sign-off must pass before the irreversible release

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-stakes or irreversible communication is about to be sent fast without review
dominance_rules.rule: verification and required sign-off dominate the pressure to send quickly
dominance_rules.required_action: run the accuracy check and obtain sign-off before release
dominance_rules.example: an external pricing email queued without a number-check

dominance_rules.trigger: persuasive framing would hide or distort a material cost or risk
dominance_rules.rule: evidence integrity dominates; framing may organize but not misrepresent
dominance_rules.required_action: disclose the material risk/cost and frame around the truth
dominance_rules.example: a proposal omitting a known recurring cost

dominance_rules.trigger: visual simplification would distort the data
dominance_rules.rule: honest data encoding dominates aesthetic simplification
dominance_rules.required_action: restore honest scales and a comparison-appropriate chart
dominance_rules.example: a truncated axis exaggerating a difference

dominance_rules.trigger: softening for tone would make the message ambiguous
dominance_rules.rule: an unambiguous message dominates; tone is tuned within that bound
dominance_rules.required_action: keep the ask explicit; adjust only surrounding tone
dominance_rules.example: a diplomatic note where the actual request is unclear

dominance_rules.trigger: a node is sequenced by perceived value ahead of an unmet prerequisite
dominance_rules.required_action: order by true prerequisite first, then by importance
dominance_rules.example: drafting before the governing message is fixed

dominance_rules.trigger: a document is being locked before its accuracy review passes
dominance_rules.rule: QA dominates lock progression; no release before review passes
dominance_rules.required_action: hold the lock until accuracy and sign-off gates pass
dominance_rules.example: hard-locking a report with unverified figures

dominance_rules.trigger: a high-risk node (risk_if_wrong>=0.80) or external irreversible release is reached
dominance_rules.rule: human review dominates automation at high-risk and irreversible gates
dominance_rules.required_action: require human sign-off before finalizing high-risk artifacts
dominance_rules.example: auto-sending a board recommendation without review

dominance_rules.trigger: applying every reviewer comment would dissolve the governing message
dominance_rules.rule: the governing message dominates literal comment application
dominance_rules.required_action: reconcile comments to the purpose; accept/reject/merge with reasons
dominance_rules.example: rewriting a clear ask into committee mush

dominance_rules.trigger: a numeric estimate is being presented as more certain than its heuristic basis
dominance_rules.rule: correct evidence labeling dominates false numeric precision
dominance_rules.required_action: label heuristic estimates as heuristic and avoid implied certainty
dominance_rules.example: quoting a made-up conversion rate as fact

dominance_rules.trigger: an audience-specific version would contradict the canonical source
dominance_rules.rule: the canonical source dominates; adaptations are derived views
dominance_rules.required_action: reconcile the adaptation to the canonical source of truth
dominance_rules.example: two audience versions stating different facts

anti_rework_rules.rule: fix audience, purpose, and message before drafting any prose
blocked_until: audience profile and governing message recorded
anti_rework_rules.rationale: drafting for an unknown reader or message forces a full rewrite
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: prose drafted before the reader is known
anti_rework_rules.example: writing a full memo then learning it was for a different audience

anti_rework_rules.rule: build the argument tree before writing body paragraphs
anti_rework_rules.rationale: writing paragraphs before grouping causes reordering and buried ledes
anti_rework_rules.example: drafting sections that later must be regrouped

anti_rework_rules.rule: set the governing message before choosing and producing a format
anti_rework_rules.rationale: format work on an unsettled message is redone when the message changes
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: format built before the message is fixed
anti_rework_rules.example: re-laying-out a deck after the recommendation changes

anti_rework_rules.rationale: cutting before clarifying can delete content that was only unclear, not unneeded
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: needed content cut as if it were filler
anti_rework_rules.example: removing a caveat that was merely poorly worded

anti_rework_rules.rule: adapt to audience and tone after the clarity pass
anti_rework_rules.rationale: tuning unclear text means editing the same sentences twice
anti_rework_rules.example: adapting jargon-heavy text then re-clarifying it

anti_rework_rules.rule: back every major claim before finalizing a report or proposal
anti_rework_rules.rationale: finalizing unsupported claims forces rework when challenged
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: a claim is finalized then found unsupported
anti_rework_rules.example: approving a proposal whose numbers cannot be sourced

anti_rework_rules.rule: write the executive summary from the validated structure, not before it
anti_rework_rules.rationale: a summary written before the body drifts out of sync
anti_rework_rules.example: summary promising a conclusion the analysis never reaches

anti_rework_rules.rule: produce charts and slides after the content and storyline are stable
anti_rework_rules.rationale: rebuilding visuals after edits is expensive and error-prone
anti_rework_rules.example: redrawing a deck each time the body changes

anti_rework_rules.rule: reconcile all feedback before the final proofreading pass
anti_rework_rules.rationale: proofreading before feedback is applied wastes the pass
anti_rework_rules.violation_signal: text proofed then changed by late feedback
anti_rework_rules.example: proofing a draft a reviewer then heavily edits

anti_rework_rules.rule: pass accuracy review and sign-off before any irreversible release
anti_rework_rules.rationale: released errors are costly to retract and damage credibility
anti_rework_rules.example: sending an external report with an unverified figure
